arXiv:2609.33334v1 [cs.LG] 27 Sep 2026

When to Evict, Not What to Keep:
Draft-Guided Eviction
for Training-Free KV-Cache Compression

Haeyong Kang Chang D. Yoo Duksung Women’s University KAIST ††thanks: Corresponding author: hykang@duksung.ac.kr.
Abstract

Training-free KV-cache compression methods such as SnapKV, H2O, and PyramidKV evict tokens at the end of prefill, aiming to preserve the attention mass that future queries are expected to use—optimizing what to keep. We show that this objective fails in two distinct ways. (1) Compensation: restoring the evicted attention mass can recover the attention-level target without recovering task quality. (2) Selection: covering more of the true decode-query mass can hurt quality when the recovered mass is fragmented rather than concentrated in coherent spans. These failures share a common cause: eviction occurs before the queries that determine the answer trajectory exist. We propose Draft-Guided Eviction (Dge), which defers eviction until after drafting the first k=2k{=}2 answer tokens using the full cache—just one decode step beyond prefill. Because the draft is generated from the answer’s own prefix, no cache entries are discarded before this trajectory signal becomes available. The per-head cache budget remains unchanged, and Dge can be applied directly to SnapKV, PyramidKV, H2O, and StreamingLLM without modifying their eviction scores. Unlike extra-pass methods, Dge changes when eviction occurs rather than what cache entries are selected. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Dge outperforms prior methods at every evaluated budget on five of six instruct-tuned backbones, achieving 44.244.2 on LongBench, nearly matching FullKV at 44.344.3. The timing-only control Dge-W achieves the same score, demonstrating that the gain comes from when eviction occurs rather than what is selected—an effect we term trajectory anchoring.

1 Introduction

Serving long-context LLMs is a memory problem before it is a compute problem: the KV-Cache grows linearly with context length and batch size—roughly 1616 GiB for an 8B model at 128K tokens, on par with the weights themselves—and every decode step reads the cache back. Training-free eviction is an attractive deployment strategy: keep a small per-head budget of BB past tokens, discard the rest, and change nothing else about the model. A productive line of work has refined which tokens to keep—StreamingLLM keeps attention sinks and recency (Xiao et al., 2024), H2O accumulates attention mass (Zhang et al., 2023), SnapKV max-pools the scores of a late-prompt observation window (Li et al., 2024), and PyramidKV schedules the budget across layers (Cai et al., 2024)—but these methods share one recipe: when prefill ends, score the past tokens, keep the top-BB per head, and evict the rest, permanently and before the first answer token is generated.

Two choices distinguish these training-free regimes: which queries score the cache, and when the cut fires. FullKV in Figure 1(a) uses the real decode queries and never evicts; prefill-time eviction in Figure 1(b) cuts before generation using only prefill-time scores; Lookahead Q-Cache (LAQ) in Figure 1(c) also cuts at prefill, but replaces future decode queries with synthesized pseudo-queries (Wang et al., 2025). Our Draft-Guided Eviction (Dge), in Figure 1(d), instead drafts the first kk answer tokens on the full cache and evicts only afterward. It therefore observes the real decode queries before making the irreversible cut: Dge changes when the cut happens, rather than what scores the cache.

Despite these differences, existing approaches optimize a common implicit objective: preserve the attention mass that future computation would place on the discarded tokens. Selection maximizes captured mass, as in SnapKV and H2O (Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023); compensation attempts to restore what selection loses through merging entries or fitting biases and values (Zhang et al., 2024b; Wan et al., 2024b; Zweiger et al., 2026); and allocation redistributes the budget across heads and layers (Feng et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024). This objective is plausible, and its attention-level gains are real. However, whether increasing attention-mass preservation reliably translates into task quality has not been systematically examined under controlled dosage.

Our controlled observations reveal two limitations. (1) Compensation: mass is fungible, but content is not. Restoring evicted attention mass through merging, value absorption, or per-token correction does not necessarily recover the information carried by the original tokens. (2) Selection: more captured attention mass does not necessarily improve task performance. When retained mass is fragmented rather than concentrated in coherent spans, an extractive answer can lose the information needed for reconstruction. We establish both effects under controlled dosage in §4, with the corresponding sweeps in Figure 2(a). Both limitations arise because eviction occurs before the queries that actually consume the cache exist: prefill-time signals can only estimate future decode queries, however they are constructed.

We propose Dge, which changes when eviction occurs rather than what is kept. Prior methods improve what a prefill-time cut keeps, while leaving the cut at the end of prefill (Kim et al., 2025; Zweiger et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). Dge instead drafts the first kk answer tokens on the full cache and evicts only afterward, allowing the decision to use real decode queries rather than estimates. The draft is the answer’s own prefix, not an auxiliary pass, so the per-head budget is unchanged and eviction leaves the prefill critical path. A single decode step is often sufficient, and §6 shows that the deferral itself, rather than a sharper selection signal, drives the gain. We attribute this to what we call trajectory anchoring: the initial answer tokens, produced on the full cache, fix the model’s decoding trajectory before compression, and the compressed cache then carries the rest, as Figure 2(b) shows.

Contributions.

  • •

    Draft-guided eviction. We introduce Dge, a training-free KV-cache compression framework that opens a new when-to-evict axis: the model first drafts kk answer tokens with the full cache and evicts only afterward, keeping the per-head budget and leaving the scoring rule a free slot—the base evictor’s own (the timing-only control Dge-W) or the draft’s real queries (the default).

  • •

    Controlled analysis of attention-based eviction. We identify two failure modes of optimizing attention mass—compensation and selection—and show that attention-level preservation can decouple from downstream task quality under controlled dosage.

  • •

    Empirical validation. Across six instruct-tuned backbones from 3B to 14B parameters, Dge outperforms prior methods at every evaluated budget on five backbones and achieves an average LongBench score of 44.244.2, compared with 40.140.1 for LAQ and 35.335.3 for SnapKV, within 0.20.2 of uncompressed FullKV. The same deferral lifts PyramidKV, H2O, and StreamingLLM, while Dge-W also reaches 44.244.2, isolating eviction timing as the source of the gain.

2 Related Work

Selection and allocation: which tokens to keep.

The dominant training-free family scores past tokens at the end of prefill under a per-head budget. SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) max-pools observation-window scores; H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) and ScissorHands (Liu et al., 2023) accumulate attention; FastGen (Ge et al., 2024) adapts budgets per head; PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2024) schedules them across layers; AdaKV (Feng et al., 2024) and HeadKV (Fu et al., 2024) reallocate them across heads; and StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2024), ThinK (Xu et al., 2024), L2L_{2} selection (Devoto et al., 2024), and Quest (Tang et al., 2024) use sinks, recency, or key statistics. These methods improve which tokens survive, but commit before the first answer token exists. Dge leaves the per-head budget unchanged and can leave the scoring rule unchanged too, deferring the same selection decision until after the initial answer tokens. On SnapKV’s own scores, this timing change alone already outperforms the selection rules we evaluate.

Compensation: restoring what selection discarded.

A second line of work attempts to repair the cut rather than improve selection. CaM (Zhang et al., 2024b), LOOK-M (Wan et al., 2024b), KVMerger (Wang et al., 2024), and D2O (Wan et al., 2024a) merge evicted entries into retained ones, with the vision analogue ToMe (Bolya et al., 2023); FAST (Zweiger et al., 2026) instead fits per-token biases and refits values. These methods can restore the attention mass targeted by the repair, but they cannot recover the original token-level content once it has been compressed away. Our controlled counterparts in §4 expose this gap: attention-level compensation can improve without a corresponding gain in task quality. Dge avoids the repair problem altogether by generating the steering tokens while the cache is still intact, so the information needed to anchor the answer trajectory is never discarded.

Extra passes: sharpening the prefill-time signal.

A third line spends additional computation to improve the eviction signal. KVzip (Kim et al., 2025) repeats the prefill pass; FAST, above, calibrates its biases and values on self-generated Q&A; LAQ (Wang et al., 2025) synthesizes pseudo future queries; and LookaheadKV (Ahn et al., 2026) trains adapters to predict such scores. These methods improve what to keep, but retain the same schedule: the cut still fires at prefill end, so the signal remains a proxy for the queries that actually consume the cache. Our experiments show that a matched LAQ run saturates with dose and, even at its best, trails a pure timing change. Other KV-efficiency methods change the representation, memory management, or decoding objective, including learned compression (Zhang et al., 2024a; Nawrot et al., 2024; Mu et al., 2023), quantization (Liu et al., 2024b; Hooper et al., 2024), PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023), InfiniGen (Lee et al., 2024), and speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023); concurrent analyses also question the attention-mass objective itself (Feng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). In contrast, Dge changes only the timing of eviction, using the answer’s own prefix to expose real decode queries before the cut; App. F contrasts it with the draft-like designs.

3 Preliminaries

Notation.

A prompt of length LL is prefilled; eviction keeps a per-head budget of BB tokens (B−wB{-}w selected past tokens plus the last ww window tokens, w=8w{=}8 throughout) per layer. For a future query qq, the full attention output decomposes exactly as

O⁡(q)=(1−β⁡(q))​Okeep​(q)+β⁡(q)​Vevict​(q),β⁡(q)=∑j∈Eaj​(q),O(q)\;=\;(1-\beta(q))\,O_{\mathrm{keep}}(q)\;+\;\beta(q)\,V_{\mathrm{evict}}(q),\qquad\beta(q)=\textstyle\sum_{j\in E}a_{j}(q), (1)

where EE is the evicted set: β\beta is the missed mass and VevictV_{\mathrm{evict}} the attention-weighted centroid of evicted values. Every compensation method estimates terms of Eq. 1; every selection method minimizes β\beta.

Held-out instrumentation.

Our diagnostics run the model once with the full cache, capture post-RoPE Q,K,VQ,K,V via forward pre-hooks, and replay real decode queries against candidate caches offline. Metrics, per App. B and H: missed decode mass βdec\beta_{\mathrm{dec}} is the β\beta of Eq. 1 on a held-out half of the decode steps, and a rule’s held-out coverage Δ\Delta is its relative reduction in βdec\beta_{\mathrm{dec}} vs SnapKV. Also relative attention-output error, retained-mask run length, and a train-free attention-matching loss |log⁡Z−log⁡Z^||\log Z-\log\hat{Z}|, the log-partition deficit between the softmax normalizer ZZ over all keys and Z^\hat{Z} over the retained ones.

Evaluation protocol.

LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) (16 English datasets) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), budgets B∈{32,64,128}B\in\{32,64,128\} (larger only in the offline diagnostics), greedy decoding, the stop-token-corrected Llama-3 chat protocol of App. A; matched sample sets across methods. Backbone checks span Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (Jiang et al., 2023), Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3-8B-Instruct, reported in Table 2 and App. D. Re-runs are bit-identical, so the only uncertainty is sampling over the 3,7503{,}750 examples; comparisons use a paired bootstrap, whose intervals on differences are ∼±0.3\sim\pm 0.3 against ±1.1\pm 1.1 marginally, as App. I details.

Headline diagnostic.

At a per-head budget of B=128B{=}128 tokens, SnapKV misses βdec=16.7%\beta_{\mathrm{dec}}=16.7\% of decode attention mass on average, with a median of 9.4%9.4\% and a 9090th percentile of 43%43\% over examples, layers and heads, a heavy tail; the window-query β\beta correlates 0.720.72 with βdec\beta_{\mathrm{dec}} (0.680.68–0.760.76 over B=64B{=}64–10241024)—the missed mass is apparent headroom that §4’s analysis shows is not convertible into task quality by content-side means.

4 Attention-Mass Analysis

We test the attention-mass objective under increasing dosage on each axis (Llama-3.1-8B, B=128B{=}128 unless a budget is named). Figure 2(a) plots each mechanism’s attention-level metric against its LongBench Δ\Delta vs SnapKV: the four what-axis mechanisms gain 88–57%57\% on their objective yet at most +0.6+0.6 on LongBench, LAQ’s 1616 pseudo queries buy +2.0+2.0, and deferring the cut by the same 1616 tokens adds a further +2.0+2.0—both Dge points near 2×2\times the best prior. Every family meets its objective and none of it transfers (Table 1(a) fit, (b) select).

Compensation restores mass, not content.

Table 1(a) is ours throughout: compensation token and multi-centroid following LOOK-M/KVMerger (Wan et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024), value absorption following CaM (Zhang et al., 2024b), per-token bias following FAST (Zweiger et al., 2026). Mechanistically (App. C), renormalized mass flows multiplicatively (inflow corr. 0.970.97 with a token’s own attention, so merging by key similarity cannot route it), post-RoPE key averaging loses 30%30\% of key norm to phase interference, and a per-token least-squares fit overfits the eight window queries a prefill affords.

Selection trades coverage for contiguity.

SnapKV’s max-pooling loses 99–22%22\% held-out coverage across B=64B{=}64–512512 yet wins scores by buying span contiguity, and raw “no pooling” inverts both at B=128B{=}128 in Table 1(b). Oracle bounds cap every practical rule (token oracle +31.8%+31.8\%; block and segment oracles in App. C). The only signal materially above the window is real decode queries: +16.5%+16.5\% in Table 1(b) (Dge16’s k=16k{=}16 draft queries, matching LAQ’s m=16m{=}16), +30.4%+30.4\% at B=512B{=}512, against +1.2%+1.2\% for lookahead’s pseudo queries in App. L. It is also the only entry in Table 1 whose gain reaches the score: with runs as short as no pooling’s (1.61.6 vs 1.81.8) it gains +3.98+3.98 where no pooling loses 1.731.73—because it is a cut deferred until the real queries exist (§5), not a better prefill-time rule: the timing-only control, keeping SnapKV’s long runs, gains the same (+3.95+3.95, Dge-W16). Figure 2(b) cashes it out: SnapKV collapses on long-form generation, and SKV+Dge2 recovers FullKV in both regimes.

5 Draft-Guided Eviction

The two problems of §4 share a cause: the cut fires before the queries that matter exist. Dge removes the cause rather than either symptom by making the real decode queries exist before the cut, and both problems then dissolve: nothing is left to compensate, and the coverage–contiguity trade-off is an artifact of pre-generation scoring—once the queries reading the cache are the real ones, the spans an extractive answer copies have already been read.

Policy.

Dge is a scheduling change, not a new scorer: it defers eviction past the opening of the generation, as App. E sets out:

  1. 1.

    Draft (phase A). Prefill normally; generate the first kk answer tokens with the full cache, capturing the kk real decode queries per layer through forward pre-hooks—no extra pass, the draft being the beginning of the final answer. Prefill’s own forward emits token one, so k=1k{=}1 is the base evictor and k=2k{=}2 the minimal dose, used throughout.

  2. 2.

    Evict (phase B). Score every past token, keep the per-head budget, and edit the cache in place—once, irrevocably. The scorer is a free slot. By default Dge uses the mean attention the kk draft queries pay to each token, which the draft provides at no cost; the timing-only Dge-W keeps the base evictor’s own scorer—SnapKV’s window, PyramidKV’s layer budgets, H2O’s accumulator or StreamingLLM’s sinks—unchanged.

  3. 3.

    Continue. Resume on the compressed cache, keeping the draft tokens as ordinary output.

§6 finds the two scorers equivalent on average: the contribution is when the cut fires. The change is correspondingly small to deploy: two stock generate() calls around one in-place cache edit, with no training, no extra pass, and no hyper-parameter beyond kk (App. E).

Cost.

Dge leaves the asymptotic peak unchanged, as Figure 3(a) sketches, and the dose itself is free: total latency is flat in kk. The cost is one cache surgery, 1.45×1.45\times on short answers and 1.02×1.02\times on long in Table 3(b), against a TTFT of 0.93×0.93\times SnapKV’s that no score-based prior evictor there beats. If the answer terminates within the draft, no eviction occurs and the output is bit-identical to FullKV’s—the rational policy, since the cache is freed at answer end.

A hypothesis for why Dge works: trajectory anchoring.

The first kk tokens are the generation’s high-information steering segment: for extractive QA they contain the copied span; for summarization they fix topic and structure. The draft segment is also precisely where prefill-time eviction bites. Produced from the whole cache, the draft anchors a trajectory a compressed cache then carries—consistent with the timing-only Dge-W matching the 44.244.2 average of Dge across Table 2 and carrying nearly all of the recovery in Figure 3(b), as §6 attributes.

6 Experiments

§4 closed the what axis; this section measures what §5’s deferral buys on the when axis: a lead over every prior method in every backbone ×\times budget cell, FullKV parity within noise, and, through a timing-only control, the deferral itself as the cause.

6.1 Experimental setup

Backbone LLMs.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024) is the primary backbone, with replications on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (Jiang et al., 2023), Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024) and Llama-3.2-3B in Table 2, and on Llama-3-8B in App. D; decoding and prompt protocol follow §3’s preliminaries.

Datasets.

We use LongBench (Bai et al., 2024), evaluating all 16 English datasets: single-document QA (NarrativeQA, Qasper, MultiFieldQA; Kočiský et al., 2018; Dasigi et al., 2021), multi-document QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue; Yang et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2022), summarization (GovReport, QMSum, MultiNews; Huang et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2021; Fabbri et al., 2019), few-shot learning (TREC, TriviaQA, SAMSum; Li and Roth, 2002; Joshi et al., 2017; Gliwa et al., 2019), synthetic retrieval and counting, and code completion (LCC, RepoBench-P; Guo et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a). Inputs average 1,235–18,409 tokens; longer prompts are middle-truncated per the official protocol, and each set is scored by its official metric (F1, ROUGE-L, accuracy, edit similarity).

Baselines.

All baselines keep the same per-layer, per-head KV budget BB and differ only in their retention strategy; our reproductions at B=128B{=}128 rank as published (SnapKV 42.242.2, PyramidKV 41.641.6, StreamingLLM 36.536.5):

  • •

    FullKV (FKV) caches every token and is the uncompressed reference.

  • •

    StreamingLLM (SLM) (Xiao et al., 2024) keeps attention sinks and a recency window only.

  • •

    SnapKV (SKV) (Li et al., 2024) scores past tokens with an observation window and max-pools before per-head top-BB; it is the base of all our variants.

  • •

    PyramidKV (PKV) (Cai et al., 2024) adds a layer-decaying budget schedule.

  • •

    Lookahead Q-Cache (LAQ) (Wang et al., 2025), the closest prior extra-pass baseline, at its best dose (m=16m{=}16) in Table 2, across doses in Table 3(a) and over the full grid in App. K.

Our variants.

Each variant is prefixed with the base evictor it modifies and keeps its budget; the suffixes isolate the two axes of §5 (pseudocode in App. E):

  • •

    SKV+Dgek (eviction timing ++ signal) is the default of §5: the cut moves to decode step kk and is scored by the kk real draft queries rather than the observation window. Budget and allocation stay SnapKV’s, so any difference from the SKV row comes from those two changes alone.

  • •

    SKV+Dge-Wk (timing only) defers eviction identically but scores with SnapKV’s unmodified window recipe, so Dge-W differs from the SKV row solely in the step at which eviction happens.

The deferral composes with the other retention rules the same way (PKV+/H2O+/SLM+Dge rows, App. K).

Unless noted otherwise: budget B=128B{=}128 for single-budget results (B∈{32,64,128}B\in\{32,64,128\} in Table 2), observation window w=8w{=}8, pooling kernel 7, draft length k=2k{=}2 (kk up to 3232 in the dose grid), matched sample sets across methods, one run per configuration (greedy; CIs in App. I).

6.2 Main results

Dge leads every prior method at every budget, near FullKV.

Averaged over all fifteen backbone ×\times budget cells, as in the Avg. column of Table 2, SKV+Dge2 scores 44.1744.17 against 40.1340.13 for the strongest prior method, SKV+LAQ at its best dose, and 35.3435.34 for SnapKV; both Dge variants beat every prior method in all fifteen cells, by at least 1.011.01, and stay within 0.770.77 of FullKV—matching or exceeding it in five cells—where the strongest prior method trails FullKV by 1.51.5–9.09.0 (per-dataset scores: App. K, except Mistral-7B and Llama-3.2-3B at B=32B{=}32). The deferral is essentially budget-invariant: averaged over backbones, as BB shrinks from 128128 to 3232, SKV+Dge2 moves only from 44.3044.30 to 44.0444.04, while SnapKV falls from 39.0639.06 to 31.0631.06, so Dge’s lead over the best prior method grows from 1.11.1–2.22.2 at B=128B{=}128 to 5.75.7–8.68.6 at B=32B{=}32. On the sixth backbone, Llama-3-8B, a k=32k{=}32 draft closes 72%72\% of the SnapKV gap to FullKV at B=128B{=}128, as App. D shows. The deferral also composes with other base evictors: PKV/H2O/SLM+Dge2 land within 0.90.9 of FullKV in the three settings App. L reports, SLM gaining +12.3+12.3 on average (PKV’s non-monotone Qwen columns: a discrete-schedule artifact, explained there too).

Where the gain lives.

Draft termination (answers ending inside the draft) is rare at the headline dose—11.2%11.2\% of samples at k=2k{=}2, 0%0\% on the long-generation categories, per App. K—so the gain must come from generation on the compressed cache. On gov_report, where ∼\sim99% of tokens decode after eviction, SKV+Dge2 lifts ROUGE-L from 22.322.3 to 32.632.6 against FullKV’s 33.833.8 (Figure 4(b)); on qmsum both deferred variants beat FullKV (App. K). The opening tokens, not the retained content, carry the generation. Off LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack (Qwen2.5-7B, B=32B{=}32)—where a query-aware selector should simply keep the needle—makes the same point: SnapKV recovers 74.774.7 and H2O 42.142.1, while Dge2 returns 100.0100.0 against FullKV’s 98.998.9 (App. J).

6.3 Attribution ablation

The attribution rests on the timing-only control Dge-W of §6.1, which splits Dge’s recovery into a pure timing term, SnapKV to Dge-W, and a pure signal term, Dge-W to Dge. On the matched 50-sample gov_report split of Figure 3(b): Δ⁡(timing)=Dge-W−S​n​a​p​K​V=+11.0\Delta(\text{timing})=\textsc{Dge}\text{-W}-SnapKV=+11.0 and Δ⁡(signal)=Dge−Dge-W=+0.7\Delta(\text{signal})=\textsc{Dge}-\textsc{Dge}\text{-W}=+0.7—timing accounts for 94%94\% of the recovery. The split holds across Table 2: averaged over all fifteen cells, deferring eviction alone lifts SnapKV from 35.3435.34 to Dge-W’s 44.1744.17, and swapping in the real decode queries adds nothing further, Dge also averaging 44.1744.17. On Llama-3.1-8B at B=128B{=}128, App. I’s paired bootstrap separates the timing gain of +4.11+4.11 from zero but not the 0.040.04 signal term. The eviction signal—the axis every selection method optimizes—is thus worth at most 0.440.44 LongBench points in any cell of Table 2 once the cut is deferred: the deferral is the effect. Hence §5’s free scorer slot: the draft queries cost nothing, and the base evictor’s own scores do as well on average—in the few cells where App. I’s bootstrap separates the two, Dge-W is ahead (Qwen2.5-14B at B≤64B{\leq}64).

6.4 Dose-response in kk

One decode step is the whole dose, as Figure 4(a) shows on every backbone but Llama-3-8B (App. D; why the dose is backbone-dependent: App. L). At B=128B{=}128 on Llama-3.1-8B, the one backbone the full grid of Table 13 (App. K) covers, k=2/4/8/16/32k{=}2/4/8/16/32 score 46.37/46.29/46.12/46.19/46.1346.37/46.29/46.12/46.19/46.13. The minimal dose k=2k{=}2 (§5) already jumps +4.2+4.2 from SnapKV and stays flat within noise thereafter, with or without the draft-query scores (Dge-W16: 46.1746.17). The pattern is budget-invariant: at B=32B{=}32 the dose is flat from k=2k{=}2 (Table 13) despite SnapKV collapsing to 35.8535.85. This flatness, and Dge-W tracking Dge although its scorer never sees the draft, are consistent with App. E.1’s eviction-mass argument.

6.5 Lookahead-query eviction

LAQ (Wang et al., 2025) scores with mm pseudo future queries but still evicts at prefill end—the what axis at its limit. Run in its own code base under our matched protocol, its dose saturates ∼\sim2 points below FullKV. Dge-W2 defers one decode step and clears LAQ’s best dose by +2.1+2.1 at B=128B{=}128 in Table 3(a), and by +5.8+5.8 at B=32B{=}32 (App. L): tighter budgets widen the gap, and Figure 4(b) places the margin on the hard summarization and code sets. Across all fifteen backbone ×\times budget cells, the Avg. column of Table 2 puts the margin at +4.0+4.0.

6.6 Complexity and overheads

Table 3(b) prices the deferral (dd: head dimension): TTFT improves to 0.93×0.93\times SnapKV’s, since eviction leaves the prefill path, and the one-off cache surgery costs 1.45×1.45\times on 3232-token answers (H2O’s accumulator: 2.15×2.15\times), amortising to 1.02×1.02\times by 512512.

7 Discussion

Sharper benchmarking.

The standard protocol—evict at end-of-prefill, then generate—folds two decisions into one number; one deferred-eviction row separates them, and averaged over backbones and budgets a timing-only deferral closes almost all of the SnapKV-to-FullKV gap of Table 2: the reported penalty is timing, not selection quality.

What the objective measures.

Attention-output fidelity is a geometric quantity §4’s mechanisms already deliver near their ceilings; task quality asks instead for retrievable content and a stable trajectory.

Limitations and research directions.

Trajectory anchoring is inferred from ablations, not isolated, and decoding is greedy throughout, so how far it survives sampling is open. LongBench’s short answers cap the doses it can probe—at k=16k{=}16 a third of Llama-3.1-8B’s answers terminate inside the draft—pointing at long-form, agentic and multilingual workloads. The draft holds the full cache, so the prototype’s working set is 2×2\times FullKV’s (1.13×1.13\times in the native GQA layout, App. G); batching it in a paged-attention server would turn the TTFT gain into throughput.

8 Conclusion

Training-free KV-cache compression evicts at the end of prefill to preserve the attention mass future queries will use—optimizing what to keep—and that objective fails in two ways: restored mass does not restore task quality, and extra coverage can hurt when it arrives fragmented. Both occur because eviction fires before the queries that will read the cache exist. Dge removes that cause by deferring eviction until after drafting the first k=2k{=}2 answer tokens on the full cache; it drops into SnapKV, PyramidKV, H2O and StreamingLLM alike, changing when eviction occurs, not what is selected. It leads every prior method at every budget on five of six backbones (44.244.2 on LongBench vs FullKV’s 44.344.3), and the timing-only control Dge-W reaches the same score: the gain is trajectory anchoring, from the deferral itself. Before optimizing what to keep, fix when to evict.

Appendix map. Appendices A and B fix the protocol behind every number: the LongBench run itself, then the offline diagnostic harness. Appendix C derives the compensation and selection mechanisms §4 analyzes and holds their two full grids, and Appendix H the attention-matching loss they optimize. Appendix E specifies Dge as pseudocode and derives a per-step eviction-mass bound that motivates why deferral can recover FullKV; Appendix F contrasts it with the other passes that also run before the cut, and Appendix G prices it in latency, TTFT and memory. Appendices D and J are the two settings the body reports only in summary—the sixth backbone and retrieval—and Appendix I the paired bootstrap behind every interval. Appendix K holds the per-dataset score tables, Appendix L the remaining ablations, and Appendix M the diagnostics that ruled a hypothesis out.

Appendix A Experimental details

Backbones and context.

We evaluate six instruct backbones. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [Dubey et al., 2024] is the primary model (128K native context via RoPE scaling); backbone checks use Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 [Jiang et al., 2023] (32K context, a different architecture family), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [Qwen Team, 2024] (a third architecture family with 28 layers and 4 KV heads, ChatML template), Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (the largest backbone, 48 layers and 8 KV heads, same ChatML protocol), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (a smaller model of the same instruct lineage, for a scale check), and Llama-3-8B-Instruct (8K native context, no RoPE scaling; the shorter-context predecessor of the primary backbone). All share the per-head KV-Cache geometry Dge operates on and differ only in long-context adaptation and instruction-tuning generation, contrasted in Table 6.

Datasets and metrics.

LongBench [Bai et al., 2024], all 16 English datasets: single-document QA (NarrativeQA, Qasper, MultiFieldQA), multi-document QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue), summarization (GovReport, QMSum, MultiNews), few-shot learning (TREC, TriviaQA, SAMSum), synthetic retrieval/counting (PassageCount, PassageRetrieval), and code completion (Lcc, RepoBench-P). We report the official per-dataset metric—F1 for QA, ROUGE-L for summarization, classification accuracy for TREC and the synthetic tasks, and edit similarity for code—and the official per-dataset max-new-token budget. Prompts exceeding the truncation limit are middle-truncated (first half ++ last half) following the official protocol; the limit is 7,5007{,}500 tokens for the Llama and Qwen backbones (matched across methods) and 31,50031{,}500 for Mistral.

Decoding and prompt protocol.

Greedy decoding throughout, so results are deterministic and there is no seed variance to average over. We use the repository’s corrected Llama-3 chat template and stop-token set (adding <|eot_id|> and a per-dataset newline stop for the few-shot sets, which otherwise over-generate); Mistral uses its [INST] wrapping. Every method sees the identical decoding pipeline and matched sample sets.

Compression settings.

Per-head budget B∈{32,64,128,512}B\in\{32,64,128,512\} (B=128B{=}128 unless noted), observation window w=8w{=}8, max-pool kernel 77 (the SnapKV recipe). The compressed cache is stored per query head (GQA layout). Dge draft length k∈{2,…,32}k\in\{2,\dots,32\} (k=2k{=}2 for both Dge and the timing-only Dge-W in the main tables, k=16k{=}16 for the two deferred markers of Figure 2(a)); at k=1k{=}1 the policy coincides with the base evictor by construction (the first token comes from the prefill forward), so k=2k{=}2—one full-cache decode step—is the smallest dose the method admits; whether it is also sufficient is backbone-dependent, as §D shows.

Software and hardware.

PyTorch with transformers 4.44.2; flash-attention 2.6.3 for the window/positional scorers and Dge, and the SDPA backend for the compensation variants (β\beta-bias and value absorption apply a decode-time attention-mask bias). Each run uses a single 80 GB GPU; all reported cells are our own runs (H2O is omitted on the Mistral-7B backbone).

Lookahead Q-Cache comparison.

We run LAQ [Wang et al., 2025] in its own released code base on the same backbone, datasets, truncation, and greedy decoding, porting in only our Llama-3 chat template and stop tokens. Without this alignment LAQ’s verbose, unterminated generations score ∼\sim5 points lower (e.g. Qasper →39.3710.96\!\to\!39.37), so the alignment is required for the matched comparison of Table 14 and §6.5.

Appendix B Diagnostic details

All diagnostics share one harness (released with the code). The model runs as plain FullKV; forward pre-hooks on every attention layer recompute post-RoPE Q,KQ,K from the layer input, so the probe observes exactly what the eviction code would see without altering the forward pass. Selection replicates SnapKV’s scoring path operation for operation—float32 softmax over the last ww queries, score sum over past keys, maxpool (kernel 77), per-head top-BB—so a rule’s diagnostic score and its deployed behavior cannot diverge through dtype or pooling drift.

The key design choice is the held-out split: every decode-step query is replayed against the full uncompressed KK, giving the attention mass a FullKV run would place on the tokens a rule evicts (βdec\beta_{\mathrm{dec}}, §4). In-window quantities (βwin\beta_{\mathrm{win}}) are what the rule can see; decode-side quantities are what it is graded on. Every selection variant in the ladder of §4 (pooling ablations, window sizes, layer-decay, key-norm re-weighting, block granularities 8/16/328/16/32, cross-layer sharing, repeat-prefill) is scored by this held-out decode coverage under identical budgets; Table 5 reports the resulting granularity ladder and Appendix M logs the rules the diagnostic ruled out.

Appendix C Compensation and selection details

Figure 5 summarizes the two key points of this section: compensation mechanisms meet their attention-level objective yet move LongBench by ∼\sim0 in Table 4, and selection rules trade held-out coverage against span contiguity—SnapKV keeps the least raw mass but the longest contiguous runs and wins scores, while raw-mass rules and oracles buy coverage by fragmenting spans in Table 5.

Mechanisms (all train-free).

(i) a single attention-matched compensation token per head (value centroid, phase-aligned key centroid, window-estimated mass target matched by key-scale search; FA2-compatible); (ii) multi-centroid variant (cc spherical-kkmeans cluster tokens); (iii) value absorption along the empirical window co-attention transport; (iv) per-token bias in the style of FAST [Zweiger et al., 2026], βi=log⁡(1+mi/si)\beta_{i}{=}\log(1+m_{i}/s_{i}) applied through the attention mask.

Baseline.

Every LongBench Δ\Delta tabulated in Tables 4 and 5, and each of the four what-axis points of Figure 2(a), save the no-pooling entry, is measured against one SnapKV run on all sixteen sets, whose average is 42.1542.15. That is 0.060.06 below the 42.2242.22 Table 3(a) and Table 2 print (42.153542.1535 against 42.216142.2161), and the gap is one of sample size rather than of runs: this run stops at 5050 of the 200200 gov_report and qmsum prompts, its predictions there are a prefix of the master sweep’s, and the two agree exactly on the other fourteen sets. Each Δ\Delta here is that variant’s own sixteen-set average minus this 42.153542.1535—the no-pooling entry, in Table 5 and in Figure 2(a) alike, excepted, its retained −1.73-1.73 coming from a 3-dataset ×\times 50 judgment run rather than a sixteen-set average—so the variant’s own number is untouched and every Δ\Delta is exactly 0.06260.0626 more generous than the same variant scored against the 42.216142.2161 run, whatever that variant’s own sample counts are (value absorption and the per-token bias are short on sets other than gov_report and qmsum). The other five points of Figure 2(a) are measured against that 42.2242.22, but only SnapKV and the two Dge markers come from the master sweep: PKV is its own 200200-prompt run and LAQ the separate code-base run Table 14 reports.

Mechanistic findings.

(a) Renormalized mass flows multiplicatively: inflow at a retained token correlates 0.970.97 with its own attention, not key similarity—so similarity-merging (LOOK-M/KVMerger; Wan et al., 2024b, Wang et al., 2024) cannot route mass correctly (kernel-transport flow corr. ≈0\approx 0). (b) Post-RoPE arithmetic key averaging loses 30%30\% of key norm to phase interference (mean per-pair resultant R≈0.33R{\approx}0.33, the whole-key norm ratio being 0.700.70); a circular-mean construction preserves it. (c) At B=128B{=}128, an unstructured least-squares value correction—the counterpart of FAST’s ordinary-least-squares CvC_{v} fit, not of its NNLS mass fit—ridge-fit on half of the real decode queries, does not transfer to the held-out half: its residual is 1.08×1.08\times the uncorrected error, so an oracle fit with B×dB{\times}d free parameters ends up worse than no correction at all. Structured closed forms have no fit to overfit. (d) Repeat-prefill queries follow induction/copy patterns (run length 1.21.2) and score selection worse than the window (−13%-13\% held-out coverage).

Compensation token (mass matching).

For evicted set EE with window-score weights wjw_{j} (∑j∈Ewj=1\sum_{j\in E}w_{j}{=}1), the token’s value is the centroid v∗=∑jwj​vjv^{\ast}=\sum_{j}w_{j}v_{j}. Its key direction is the phase-aligned centroid: each RoPE rotate-half pair (d,d+64)(d,d{+}64) is treated as a complex number zjz_{j}, and the weighted complex sum is renormalized to the weighted magnitude, z~=∑jwj​zj|∑jwj​zj|​∑jwj​|zj|\tilde{z}=\frac{\sum_{j}w_{j}z_{j}}{|\sum_{j}w_{j}z_{j}|}\sum_{j}w_{j}|z_{j}|, so the circular-mean phase is kept and no norm is lost to phase interference. (A naive arithmetic mean shrinks by the resultant length R=|∑jwj​zj|/∑jwj​|zj|∈[0,1]R=|\sum_{j}w_{j}z_{j}|/\sum_{j}w_{j}|z_{j}|\in[0,1]; RR is also our phase-dispersion measure.) The token’s target mass is β∗=βwin⋅R\beta^{\ast}=\beta_{\mathrm{win}}\cdot R (dispersed phases shrink the target), clamped to [10−4,0.5][10^{-4},0.5]. With retained log-partition log⁡Z^i\log\hat{Z}_{i} per window query ii and ci=qi⊤​u/dc_{i}=q_{i}^{\top}u/\sqrt{d} for unit key direction uu, the mass the token receives at key scale ss is σ⁡(s​ci−log⁡Z^i)¯\overline{\sigma(s\,c_{i}-\log\hat{Z}_{i})}; ss is chosen on a 129129-point grid over [0, 25/maxi⁡|ci|][0,\,25/\max_{i}|c_{i}|] (exp-safe) to match β∗\beta^{\ast}. Pure key scaling—no logit bias—so the token runs unchanged under FlashAttention-2. The multi-centroid variant first splits EE by weighted spherical kk-means (deterministic position-stratified init) and builds one token per cluster.

Value absorption and the closed-form bias.

Both use the same empirical transport: with window-attention matrix AA, co-attention Ci​j=∑wAw​i​Aw​jC_{ij}=\sum_{w}A_{wi}A_{wj} (retained ii, evicted jj), column-normalized to Tj→iT_{j\to i}. Absorption folds evicted values into retained ones, ci=vi+(∑jμj​Tj→i​vj−mi​vi)/(si+mi)c_{i}=v_{i}+\bigl(\sum_{j}\mu_{j}T_{j\to i}v_{j}-m_{i}v_{i}\bigr)/(s_{i}{+}m_{i}) with transported mass mi=∑jμj​Tj→im_{i}=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}T_{j\to i}—closed form, keys and cache shape untouched, decode unchanged. The per-token bias is the closed form βi=log⁡(1+mi/si)\beta_{i}=\log(1+m_{i}/s_{i}), clamped at 1010, added to the decode attention mask, which grows token ii’s softmax mass from sis_{i} toward si+mis_{i}{+}m_{i}. This replaces Zweiger et al. [2026]’s NNLS fit, which FAST solves on thousands of reference queries per KV-head per context—a reservoir cap of 50,00050{,}000, averaging ∼16,000{\sim}16{,}000 per head on QuALITY. Refit train-free on the w=8w{=}8 observation queries a single prefill affords, that regression can drive in-window error to zero by memorizing them, precisely the failure mode the held-out decode replay is built to catch (cf. repeat-prefill in Appendix M); the closed form has no fit to overfit, and offline replay measured 1111–14%14\% attention-output error reduction for absorption at B=128B{=}128–512512 against −1.5%-1.5\% for the bias alone, as Appendix M logs.

Appendix D The sixth backbone: Llama-3-8B and the minimal steering dose

We repeat the main experiment on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the predecessor of our primary backbone. The two models share their entire architecture and KV geometry—so Dge operates on an identical per-head cache—and differ only in long-context adaptation: Llama-3.1 adds a 16×16\times longer context via RoPE scaling and a stronger, chattier instruction-tuning round, itemized in Table 6. This isolates the effect of the backbone’s generation behavior on the deferral.

The minimal steering dose is backbone-dependent.

On Llama-3 the single-step deferral (k=2k{=}2) that erases the gap on Llama-3.1 needs a longer draft: SKV+Dge2 recovers +2.1+2.1 of the 5.85.8-point gap at B=64B{=}64 (already the best compression method in the block) and trails SnapKV by 0.770.77 at B=128B{=}128. Crucially this is not degeneration—the anchored openings are fluent and often more complete answers—but a longer draft recovers the gap: the dose climbs monotonically →→→→42.7339.73\!\to\!40.88\!\to\!42.09\!\to\!42.38\!\to\!42.73 at k=2/4/8/16/32k{=}2/4/8/16/32. There is no knee—each extra anchor token buys a little more, with 79%79\% of the total climb done by k=8k{=}8 and the remaining 0.640.64 spread over k=→32k{=}8\!\to\!32—and the ramp only overtakes SnapKV itself between k=2k{=}2 (−0.77-0.77 against the 40.5040.50 baseline) and k=4k{=}4 (+0.38+0.38). SKV+Dge32 (42.7342.73) is the best compression method in the block, above SnapKV 40.5040.50 and recovering 72%72\% of the 3.083.08-point gap to FullKV 43.5843.58 (large per-dataset jumps: Qasper →42.535.1\!\to\!42.5, SAMSum →42.739.0\!\to\!42.7). Two consequences: the headline k=2k{=}2 result is a property of decisive-opening backbones (the modern long-context generation), and the §4 analysis is unaffected, having been measured on Llama-3.1. An answer-length-controlled rescore separates the verbosity artifact from the real deficit on the worst case, TriviaQA: SKV++Dge2’s first-line score is 75.875.8 against 89.889.8 (SnapKV) and 90.690.6 (Dge16)—the k=2k{=}2 draft leaves Llama-3 mid-preamble, and its chattier full-sentence openings (“United States of America.” where the reference is “United States”) are scored down by extractive F1. Truncating each first line to the longest reference length (+2+2 words) recovers +5.9+5.9 for Dge2 (→81.775.8\!\to\!81.7) while moving every other method ≤1.0\leq\!1.0 and Llama-3.1’s Dge2 by 0.10.1 (→92.692.5\!\to\!92.6): roughly 40%40\% of the deficit is phrasing, and the residual ∼\sim99 points is what Table 7’s longer drafts close (90.390.3 at k=8k{=}8).

What the dose actually measures.

A larger kk changes two things at once: the scorer sees more real decode queries, and more tokens are generated before the cut. Three probes separate them, and only the second of the two survives.

(i) It is not a slower start. The natural reading of “longer steering segment” is that Llama-3 takes more tokens to reach its answer. It does not. Scoring the FullKV generations of both backbones for the token position at which a gold answer string first appears—six extractive LongBench sets, 505505 and 550550 predictions in which a gold string appears at all—gives a median onset of 00 tokens on both, with 92%92\% (Llama-3) and 98%98\% (Llama-3.1) of answers begun within two tokens. The chattier phrasing documented above is real, but it does not delay the answer.

(ii) It is not slower selection convergence. If the dose bought scoring information, Llama-3’s chosen tokens should keep moving for longer. We replayed Dge’s own scoring path—mean softmax attention of the first kk draft queries over past keys, group-meaned across GQA heads, per-head top-BB—and measured the overlap between the set kept at kk and the set kept at k=32k{=}32, over six datasets (6363 and 6464 prompts). The two backbones are indistinguishable: 0.6050.605 (Llama-3) vs 0.6110.611 (Llama-3.1) at k=2k{=}2, and 0.8580.858 vs 0.8380.838 at k=16k{=}16. Selection converges at the same rate on both.

(iii) It is consistent with anchoring. The discriminating run is the timing-only control at the same doses. Dge-W2, Dge-W16 and Dge-W32 keep SnapKV’s window scores—the draft contributes no scoring information whatsoever—yet they climb →→42.6139.81\!\to\!42.19\!\to\!42.61 at k=2/16/32k{=}2/16/32, landing within 0.080.08, 0.190.19 and 0.120.12 of full Dge at each dose in Table 7. The dose does not buy a better eviction signal; it buys tokens generated on the full cache before the cut. Llama-3’s trajectory simply takes longer to become robust to eviction, which is a statement about when the cut can safely happen, not about what it should keep. Even the one parameter that looked like a scoring choice turns out to be timing.

Appendix E Draft-guided eviction implementation

Implementation notes.

Algorithm 1’s prototype is two stock generate() calls around one cache edit. Phase A lifts every layer’s max_capacity_prompt to 2302^{30} (compression disabled) and registers forward pre-hooks that recompute post-RoPE queries from each layer’s input: per-step decode queries (the eviction evidence), the last-ww prompt queries (for the Dge-W control), and, for the H2O base only, all prompt queries (its accumulator; freed per layer as consumed, ∼\sim60 MB/layer). Phase B edits the cache in place, per layer: score, top-BB, sort indices to preserve temporal order, then gather [retained past] ∥\| [window ++ draft tail]; the continuation call resumes from the edited cache (retained tokens’ RoPE positions are already baked into their cached keys, so no re-indexing is needed). Early termination: if the draft ends (EOS, or fewer than kk tokens produced), phase A’s output is returned as-is and no eviction ever fires; this is the FullKV-identical path whose per-dataset frequency Table 16 accounts. Latency and memory of the two-phase prototype are measured in App. G: +9.9%+9.9\% over SnapKV end-to-end, flat in kk, with TTFT 0.93×0.93\times.

E.1 Why deferral can recover FullKV: an eviction-mass argument

Write the per-head decode output at step tt as ot=∑jat,j​vjo_{t}=\sum_{j}a_{t,j}\,v_{j} with weights at,j=softmaxj​(qt⊤​kj/d)a_{t,j}=\mathrm{softmax}_{j}(q_{t}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}). Split the keys into the retained set RR and the evicted set EE, and let mt​(E)=∑j∈Eat,jm_{t}(E)=\sum_{j\in E}a_{t,j} be the evicted mass—the attention the step-tt query places on discarded tokens. Renormalizing over RR gives the compressed output o~t=∑j∈Rat,j1−mt​vj=μRt\tilde{o}_{t}=\sum_{j\in R}\tfrac{a_{t,j}}{1-m_{t}}v_{j}=\mu_{R}^{t}; writing μEt,μRt\mu_{E}^{t},\mu_{R}^{t} for the attention-weighted value means over E,RE,R we have ot=(1−mt)​μRt+mt​μEto_{t}=(1-m_{t})\mu_{R}^{t}+m_{t}\mu_{E}^{t}, hence

‖ot−o~t‖=mt​(E)​‖μEt−μRt‖≤ 2​mt​(E)​ρv,ρv=maxj⁡‖vj−v¯‖.\|o_{t}-\tilde{o}_{t}\|\;=\;m_{t}(E)\,\bigl\|\mu_{E}^{t}-\mu_{R}^{t}\bigr\|\;\leq\;2\,m_{t}(E)\,\rho_{v},\qquad\rho_{v}=\max_{j}\|v_{j}-\bar{v}\|. (2)

The per-step error is linear in the evicted mass mt​(E)m_{t}(E) and vanishes when mt​(E)=0m_{t}(E){=}0. Summing over decoding (errors accumulate to first order as each output feeds the next step), the end-to-end deviation is bounded by ∑tmt​(E)​‖Δ​μt‖\sum_{t}m_{t}(E)\,\|\Delta\mu_{t}\|, and the eviction time sets the summation range:

ℒS​n​a​p​K​V≈∑t=1Tmt​(Ew)​‖Δ​μt‖(cut at ​t=0),ℒDge≈∑t=k+1Tmt​(E)​‖Δ​μt‖(cut at ​t=k).\mathcal{L}_{SnapKV}\!\approx\!\!\sum_{t=1}^{T}\!m_{t}(E_{w})\|\Delta\mu_{t}\|\ \ (\text{cut at }t{=}0),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Dge}}\!\approx\!\!\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}\!m_{t}(E)\|\Delta\mu_{t}\|\ \ (\text{cut at }t{=}k). (3)

Only the per-step bound (2) is exact; three observations then suggest an ordering. (i) Termination. A dataset-dependent fraction ρ\rho of answers finishes within kk tokens (T≤kT\!\leq\!k)—11.2%11.2\% overall at k=2k{=}2, up to 92.5%92.5\% on passage_count in Table 16; for those the sum in ℒDge\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Dge}} is empty, so Dge and Dge-W equal FullKV exactly. (ii) Anchoring. For T>kT{>}k, the kk tokens y1:ky_{1:k} are produced on the full cache and their KV is kept (recent), so later queries commit to the context those tokens select and mt​(E)m_{t}(E) decays for t>kt{>}k; the deferred terms in (3) are small even for the window-chosen set EwE_{w} (this is Dge-W). (iii) Signal. Dge further picks EE to minimize ∑t≤kmt​(E)\sum_{t\leq k}m_{t}(E) from the real draft queries, which at k=16k{=}16 (Dge16) cover +16.5%+16.5\% more held-out decode mass than the window estimate (§4); this shrinks mt​(E)m_{t}(E) for t>kt{>}k a little more, but by (i)–(ii) the residual is already small, so the gain over Dge-W is second order. Together they suggest ℒS​n​a​p​K​V≥ℒDge-W≈ℒDge≥0=ℒFKV\mathcal{L}_{SnapKV}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Dge}\text{-W}}\!\approx\!\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Dge}}\geq 0=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKV}}, i.e. SKV << Dge-W ≈\approx Dge ≈\approx FullKV, consistent with the measured 42.2<≈46.19<46.2442.2<46.17\!\approx\!46.19<46.24 at k=16k{=}16 (Dge-W16 and Dge16); at the headline k=2k{=}2 both deferred rows edge past FullKV, by 0.090.09 and 0.120.12 in Table 10’s paired bootstrap, a margin it does not resolve from zero.

Why Dge and Dge-W barely differ.

The two share every step and differ only in the evicted set, so their loss gap is ℒDge-W−ℒDge=∑t>k[mt​(Ew)−mt​(E)]​‖Δ​μt‖\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Dge}\text{-W}}-\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Dge}}=\sum_{t>k}\bigl[m_{t}(E_{w})-m_{t}(E)\bigr]\|\Delta\mu_{t}\|. Two effects make this doubly small. First, by anchoring (ii) both mt​(Ew)m_{t}(E_{w}) and mt​(E)m_{t}(E) are already small for t>kt{>}k, so each summand is a difference of two small numbers. Second, the window set EwE_{w} and the draft-query set EE largely overlap: both keep the salient tokens and disagree only on the residual +16.5%+16.5\% of decode mass (k=16k{=}16), which anchoring has already made negligible after step kk. The gap is thus second order in the deferred mass, and Dge-W tracks Dge to within measurement noise (46.1746.17 vs 46.1946.19 for Dge-W16 and Dge16; Dge-W even edges Dge at B=32B{=}32 and k=2k{=}2, 46.4046.40 vs 46.3946.39 for Dge-W2 and Dge2). In one line: once the cut is deferred, which tokens are dropped barely matters—the timing has already removed the error that selection was fighting over.

Appendix F Draft-like passes compared

Several training-free compression methods insert an extra forward pass between prefill and generation because the observation window is a weak estimate of the queries the answer will actually ask. Table 8 compares them along three design choices: what the pass generates, whether its compute survives into the output, and which axis its product feeds. Repeat-prefill [Kim et al., 2025] replays the prompt and scores keys by reconstruction; self-study [Zweiger et al., 2026] generates synthetic Q&A about the context to calibrate biases and values, at an up-front per-context cost; Lookahead Q-Cache [Wang et al., 2025] synthesizes mm pseudo future queries and re-scores retention with them. All three discard the pass afterwards, and all three still cut at prefill end: the pass only sharpens what is kept. Speculative decoding [Leviathan et al., 2023] appears because Dge is mechanically closer to it than to the eviction scorers—a draft generated by the model itself, kept when it is right—but it targets latency, not memory. LookaheadKV [Ahn et al., 2026] is the trained sibling of the same what-axis move, predicting lookahead scores draft-free; we compare training-free passes only.

Dge breaks both invariants at once. Its pass is the answer’s own first kk tokens, so the compute is not an overhead to amortize but output the user receives either way; and its product is not a better score but a later cut. The ablations say the second difference is the one that pays: with SnapKV’s unmodified window scores, the timing-only Dge-W stays within 0.440.44 of full Dge in every cell of Table 2, while LAQ—a strictly richer scoring signal evicting at the old time—saturates ≥\geq2 points below the pure timing change at its best dose in Table 14. Sharpening what without moving when runs into a ceiling that one deferred step clears.

Appendix G Complexity and overheads

Table 9 reports, per method, when it evicts, the extra scoring compute, peak/decode KV memory, and measured per-sample latency relative to SnapKV. All evictors share O⁡(L)O(L) asymptotic peak memory (the end-of-prefill cache) and O⁡(B+t)O(B{+}t) decode memory; Dge changes only the eviction time, holding the full cache for kk extra decode steps before dropping to the same steady state.

Where the overhead actually goes.

To separate the method’s intrinsic cost from our prototype’s, we ran a controlled microbenchmark (Llama-3.1-8B, B=128B{=}128, a fixed 7,7627{,}762-token prompt, 256256 new tokens, 11 warm-up ++ 33 timed repeats on one A100-class GPU; Table 9’s Latency column comes from the separate LongBench probe described there and is not directly comparable). Three things follow.

(i) The dose is free. Total latency is flat in kk: 10.8810.88s, 10.4910.49s and 10.4910.49s at k=2,4,8k{=}2,4,8—a 3.7%3.7\% spread with no monotone trend, against a run-to-run σ\sigma of up to 0.230.23s. Quadrupling the draft costs nothing measurable, so the kk full-cache decode steps are not the cost driver. The overhead over SnapKV (+0.96+0.96s, +9.9%+9.9\% here) is therefore the one-off per-layer cache surgery.

(ii) TTFT improves. Because the draft runs before any eviction, the first token is produced on the uncompressed cache and the compression never sits on the prefill critical path: TTFT is 0.93×0.93\times SnapKV’s, essentially FullKV’s (0.91×0.91\times). H2O is the opposite case—its O⁡(L2)O(L^{2}) accumulator runs during prefill, giving a 3.45×3.45\times TTFT that its total latency hides whenever the generation is long (2.15×2.15\times on short answers, 1.06×1.06\times on long-form). LAQ is the same case for the same reason: its mm pseudo queries come from an extra forward pass that is discarded, so the whole pass lands before the first token. Measured under this protocol in LAQ’s own code base (m=16m{=}16, 11 warm-up ++ 55 repeats), it is 1.42×1.42\times. That code base’s SnapKV is not ours (1.0681.068 vs 1.1701.170 s), so we anchor on FullKV, unpatched in both and agreeing to 0.2%0.2\% (1.05931.0593 vs 1.06161.0616 s): LAQ is 1.561×1.561\times FullKV there and FullKV is 0.907×0.907\times SnapKV here. Dividing LAQ straight by our SnapKV gives 1.41×1.41\times, so the anchoring changes little. Dge’s draft is the answer’s opening, and is not discarded.

(iii) The real price is memory, and it is layout, not deferral. Separating the 14.9614.96 GiB of weights from the working set (KV-Cache ++ activations), the peak is 5.695.69 GiB for SnapKV, 6.586.58 GiB for FullKV and 13.1313.13 GiB for Dge2—2.0×2.0\times FullKV’s working set, and dose-independent (13.12613.126 vs 13.13213.132 GiB at k=2k{=}2 and k=8k{=}8), confirming (i): the cost is the one-off draft machinery, not holding the cache longer. The dominant term is the cache layout: to score eviction per head, this codebase repeats KV to all 3232 query heads before caching, so the uncompressed prefill cache is 3.793.79 GiB where the native 88-head GQA layout stores 0.950.95 GiB. Every evictor pays this constant, but only Dge pays it at full prompt length, because only Dge holds the cache uncompressed through the draft.

LAQ shows the same cost from the same cause. Holding the generated count fixed at 256256 on this prompt, so every method does equal work, its working set is FullKV’s, not SnapKV’s: 7.607.60 against FullKV’s 7.627.62 and SnapKV’s 5.685.68 GiB. The lookahead pass runs before any eviction, so the peak is taken on the uncompressed cache—the same structural reason its TTFT is 1.42×1.42\times. (These three are measured with the count pinned, which FullKV’s uncapped cache grows with, so its 7.627.62 is not the 6.586.58 above; SnapKV’s 5.685.68 and Dge’s 13.1113.11 reproduce the 5.695.69 and 13.1313.13 either way.)

Removing it, measured. We implemented the fix sketched in Figure 7(b): cache in the native GQA layout, score eviction with the captured query-head queries, and mean the scores over each group of 44 query heads (the codebase’s gqa_score_agg convention). Dge2’s working set drops →7.4413.13\!\to\!7.44 GiB—from 2.0×2.0\times to 1.13×1.13\times FullKV—exceeding the +2.84+2.84 GiB layout term because FlashAttention-2 consumes GQA natively, so the 3232-head expansion disappears from the compute path as well as the cache. The result is base-independent (PKV++Dge2: identical 13.12613.126/7.4397.439 GiB in the two layouts) and score-neutral on a spot check (Llama-3.1, B=128B{=}128: Qasper −0.06-0.06, TREC ±0.00\pm 0.00, SAMSum −0.34-0.34—all inside the ±0.5\pm 0.5 no-effect band). The full-suite numbers elsewhere in this paper remain in the query-head layout, the one every baseline also uses, so all comparisons stay matched; the asymptotics (O⁡(L)O(L) peak) were never at issue, and the constant is now demonstrated—not merely argued—to be a layout choice rather than a property of deferral.

Appendix H Attention-matching loss

Definition.

Fix a layer and head. A compression keeps a retained set RR of past keys and drops EE; let qq range over the observation queries—in SnapKV the ww window queries at the end of the prompt, used as an estimate of the not-yet-seen decode queries. Write the full-attention log-partition and its retained restriction as

logZ(q)=log∑j∈R∪Eeq⊤​kj/d,logZ^(q)=log∑j∈Req⊤​kj/d.\log Z(q)=\log\!\!\sum_{j\in R\cup E}\!e^{q^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}},\qquad\log\hat{Z}(q)=\log\!\!\sum_{j\in R}\!e^{q^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}}. (4)

The training-free attention-matching loss is the mean log-partition deficit, which we measure directly at compression time,

ℒmatch=𝔼q​|log⁡Z⁡(q)−log⁡Z^​(q)|=𝔼q​[−log⁡(1−ρq)],ρq=∑j∈Eeq⊤​kj/d∑j∈R∪Eeq⊤​kj/d∈[0,1),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{match}}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{q}\,\bigl|\log Z(q)-\log\hat{Z}(q)\bigr|\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{q}\,\bigl[-\log\bigl(1-\rho_{q}\bigr)\bigr],\quad\rho_{q}=\frac{\sum_{j\in E}e^{q^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}}}{\sum_{j\in R\cup E}e^{q^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d}}}\in[0,1), (5)

where ρq\rho_{q} is exactly the softmax mass the observation query places on the evicted keys—the observation-query analogue of the evicted mass mt​(E)m_{t}(E) of Equation 2. So the loss is a monotone −log(1−⋅)-\log(1-\cdot) transform of the dropped attention mass: it is zero iff the retained set carries all of qq’s attention and diverges as the evicted mass approaches one. Minimizing it over RR under a size budget is the window-query counterpart of FAST’s mass-matching objective [Zweiger et al., 2026], the one its NNLS fit solves; SnapKV’s top-BB selection on the pooled window-query scores is its greedy solution, and the per-token bias β\beta that FAST fits to reweight the retained logits shifts log⁡Z^\log\hat{Z} by exactly the recoverable part of (5) (a run with β\beta closes the deficit to 𝔼q​|log⁡Z−log⁡(Z^​eβ)|\mathbb{E}_{q}|\log Z-\log(\hat{Z}\,e^{\beta})|).

The loss does not predict the downstream deficit.

The crucial point for this paper is that (5) is an observation-query, prefill-time quantity: it scores how well RR reconstructs attention for the window queries, on the full cache, before any decoding. Equation 3 shows the error that actually accrues is ∑tmt​(Et)​‖Δ​μt‖\sum_{t}m_{t}(E_{t})\|\Delta\mu_{t}\| over the real decode queries qtq_{t}, whose weight is set by when EE is dropped, not by how well the prefill observations were matched. Figure 8 makes this quantitative at scale on Llama-3.1-8B (B=128B{=}128). Across the sixteen sets the loss varies over a narrow 2×2\times band (0.140.14–0.280.28) yet SnapKV’s deficit from FullKV ranges from −1.5-1.5 to 13.213.2 points, and the two are essentially uncorrelated (Pearson r≈0.2r{\approx}0.2, i.e. the loss explains ∼4%\sim 4\% of the deficit variance): the sets SnapKV hits hardest—Qasper (13.213.2) and GovReport (11.511.5)—sit at low-to-mid loss, while the highest-loss set (TREC, 0.280.28) loses only 77. Keeping the identical selection and evicting one decode step later (Dge-W2) drives the deficit to −0.09-0.09 on average (worst case 1.51.5) at every loss. The quantity the what-axis optimizes is orthogonal to the error the when-axis removes.

Appendix I Confidence intervals and significance

All decoding is greedy, so re-running a configuration reproduces it bit for bit and there is no seed variance to report. The uncertainty that does exist is sampling over the 3,7503{,}750 LongBench examples. We bootstrap it (20002000 resamples): within each dataset we resample examples with replacement, preserving dataset sizes, recompute each dataset score and macro-average over the 16 sets—exactly how the headline number is formed.

Comparisons use a paired bootstrap: both methods are scored on the same resample, which is legitimate because every method here is run on identical example sets, and is far sharper than comparing two marginal intervals. The distinction matters: the marginal intervals are ±1.1\pm 1.1 (dominated by which datasets are drawn), so read naively they would suggest nothing in Table 2 is resolvable, whereas the paired intervals on differences are ∼±0.3\sim\pm 0.3.

This sharpens the paper’s central claim. On Llama-3.1 the paired test says Dge2 and Dge-W2 are not distinguishable at all on 3,7503{,}750 examples, while both separate from SnapKV by ∼\sim4.14.1 with intervals nowhere near zero. Qwen2.5-14B is stricter still: at B≤64B{\leq}64 the difference between the two deferred variants does resolve, and it favors the timing-only control by 0.40.4—swapping SnapKV’s window scores for real draft queries adds no signal and, on this backbone, costs 0.40.4—while both variants stay indistinguishable from FullKV at every budget. The when axis carries a gain that survives resampling; the what axis never produces one, on either backbone.

Appendix J Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval

The LongBench averages aggregate generation quality; Figure 9 isolates retrieval under the same tight budget. We run the standard Needle-in-a-Haystack probe on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at B=32B{=}32: the needle sentence is planted at 1010 depths across 1515 context lengths (11k–88k), for 150150 probes per method, and a cell is scored by the fraction of the expected answer’s words the model recovers.

This is the regime most favorable to prefill-time eviction: the retrieval question is in the prompt, so SnapKV’s window queries can see which tokens matter, and a query-aware selector should simply keep the needle. It does not. At B=32B{=}32 SnapKV recovers only 74.774.7 against FullKV’s 98.998.9—it drops needles across the whole depth×\timeslength grid—and H2O, whose accumulated-attention rule is not query-aware, falls to 42.142.1. Deferring the same SnapKV selection by a single decode step (Dge2) restores 100.0100.0: every needle, at every depth and length. The 25.325.3-point recovery is bought without changing which tokens are scored or how, only when they are dropped—the Table 2 story reproduced on a task where the what-axis was supposed to be sufficient.

The full 16-dataset breakdown of the main results (summarized as averages in Table 2) is split for readability into the prefill-time baselines of Table 11 and the deferred-eviction rows of Table 12; the complete SnapKV-variant dose grid and the lookahead-query comparison follow.

Table 15 aggregates the 16 sets into the six standard LongBench categories, and Table 16 reports, per dataset, how often the answer finishes inside the kk-token draft—together with the sample-count check. Every configuration in these tables is run at LongBench’s full official sizes (200200 per set, 150150 for multifieldqa_en, 500500 for lcc and repobench-p; 3,7503{,}750 samples per configuration) with no subsampling; the diagnostic runs behind the grids of App. C are the exception that section records. The only truncation is the standard per-backbone context limit of App. A.

Appendix L Additional analysis

Draft-termination fractions and the two regimes.

When an answer finishes inside the kk-token draft the cache is freed at answer end, no eviction ever fires, and Dge is bit-identical to FullKV—so it is worth asking how much of Dge’s gain this path accounts for. Measuring it directly in Table 16, re-tokenizing every saved answer, shows it is a small share: at the headline dose k=2k{=}2 only 11.2%11.2\% of the 3,7503{,}750 samples terminate in the draft, and termination is confined to short-answer QA (55–40%40\%) and passage_count (92.5%92.5\%), with Summarization, Few-shot and Code at 0%0\%. Even at k=16k{=}16 the overall figure is 34.0%34.0\%. The gain therefore cannot be a draft-termination artifact: ∼\sim89% of samples at k=2k{=}2 genuinely decode on the compressed cache, and Dge2 still matches FullKV (46.3746.37 vs 46.2446.24). The cleanest case is long-form generation, where the answer far exceeds kk: on gov_report (512512-token generations, 0%0\% termination) ∼\sim99% of tokens decode on the compressed cache, so the recovery (→32.622.3\!\to\!32.6 ROUGE at B=128B{=}128) is best explained by trajectory anchoring.

Composition across retention rules.

The single full-cache decode step transfers to the three other base evictors we test, not just SnapKV: at B=128B{=}128, PKV++Dge2 reaches 46.2146.21 (from PyramidKV’s 41.6441.64), H2O++Dge2 reaches 45.7345.73 (+7.6+7.6), and StreamingLLM++Dge2 reaches 45.8345.83—a +9.3+9.3 jump for a rule that keeps four sinks and a recency window without any attention scores at all. The timing-only compositions, run in the same sweep but not tabulated, land within 0.350.35 of their draft-scored counterparts (PKV++Dge-W2 46.3846.38, H2O++Dge-W2 45.3945.39), confirming that the recovery is a property of the eviction event and not of any particular retention rule. The recovery also holds at the tightest budget: at B=32B{=}32, PKV/H2O/StreamingLLM++Dge2 reach 46.42/45.70/46.2346.42/45.70/46.23, a +12.8+12.8 jump for StreamingLLM from 33.4433.44. The same composition holds on a second backbone: on Qwen2.5-7B at B=128B{=}128, PKV++Dge2 reaches 45.0345.03 (from PyramidKV’s 38.3838.38, +6.7+6.7), H2O++Dge2 reaches 44.6744.67 (from 35.6635.66, +9.0+9.0), and StreamingLLM++Dge2 reaches 44.8644.86 (+14.7+14.7)—all within 0.90.9 of Qwen’s FullKV 45.5445.54, per Table 12.

Lookahead-query dose saturation.

LAQ’s pseudo-query dose helps but saturates ∼\sim2 points below a pure timing change. At B=128B{=}128 the m=4/8/16/32m{=}4/8/16/32 averages are 43.81/44.13/44.20/44.1043.81/44.13/44.20/44.10—the curve peaks at m=16m{=}16 and is flat (even slightly down) at m=32m{=}32, so spending more pseudo queries does not close the gap to FullKV (46.2446.24) or to Dge-W2 (46.3346.33). The same ordering holds at B=64B{=}64. The deficit against the timing-only control also widens as the budget shrinks—1.01.0–2.12.1 points at B=128B{=}128 (Qwen2.5-14B: 1.71.7) vs 3.03.0–3.93.9 at B=64B{=}64 and 5.85.8–9.19.1 at B=32B{=}32—so tighter budgets make when matter more, not less. Sharpening the what-signal has a ceiling that a single deferral step clears outright, as Table 14 shows.

What LAQ’s pseudo queries are actually worth.

The dose curve says the what-signal saturates; this probe says why. We replay LAQ’s two stages inside the selection harness of Appendix B—compress the prefill cache to BB with SnapKV (window 3232), generate m=16m{=}16 tokens on that compressed cache keeping their post-RoPE queries, then score the full prompt keys with the last 8+m8+m rows, exactly as our matched runs configure LAQ—and score the resulting selection against the same held-out decode attention every other rung of the ladder is measured on. LAQ’s pseudo queries buy +1.2%+1.2\% covered mass over SnapKV’s window estimate at B=128B{=}128 (+1.3%+1.3\% at B=64B{=}64; 1212 prompts), and −3.1%-3.1\% when the window rows are removed and the pseudo queries score alone. The real draft queries Dge captures at the same dose (k=16k{=}16, i.e. Dge16) are worth +18.7%+18.7\% on the same 1212 prompts, and the oracle +30.5%+30.5\%—the two rungs Table 1(b) reports as +16.5+16.5/+31.8%+31.8\% on its own diagnostic split, re-measured here so all three are scored on identical prompts. Generating the lookahead on a cache already compressed to BB costs essentially all of the signal the draft was supposed to provide. The pseudo continuation also leaves the real answer early—it agrees with the full-cache answer for 5.15.1 tokens on average, and on gov_report, where the compression gap lives, it diverges after one to eight. This is the measurement behind LAQ’s position in Figure 2(a): it improves its own objective by almost nothing, yet still gains +2.0+2.0 LongBench—a second, opposite reading of the miscalibration the analysis reports, and the reason the timing-only control beside it, with no signal change at all, gains twice as much.

The minimal steering dose is capability-, not scale-, dependent.

The dose kk that recovers FullKV is backbone-dependent: Llama-3.1-8B (both B=32B{=}32 and 128128), Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and the smaller Llama-3.2-3B all saturate at k=2k{=}2, whereas the older, shorter-context Llama-3-8B climbs gradually in Figure 4(a) and needs k≈8k{\approx}8, analyzed in App. D. That the 33B model still needs only k=2k{=}2 while an 88B model needs k≈8k{\approx}8 shows the dose tracks the decisiveness of a backbone’s opening tokens (how quickly its instruction tuning commits to a trajectory), not parameter count. Scaling up does not shrink the problem either: on Qwen2.5-14B—the largest backbone we run—SnapKV at B=32B{=}32 posts its largest LongBench-average collapse in the paper (29.9429.94 vs FullKV 46.0546.05, −16.1-16.1), and the same k=2k{=}2 deferral recovers 45.7445.74 in Table 12, within 0.310.31 of FullKV.

PyramidKV’s non-monotone Qwen columns are a discrete-schedule artifact.

In Table 2 PKV on Qwen2.5-7B scores lower at B=64B{=}64 (30.7430.74) than at B=32B{=}32 (32.6932.69), and Qwen2.5-14B repeats the inversion (34.6434.64 vs 35.0735.07); the runs reproduce bit-identically under greedy decoding, so it is systematic, and the cause is arithmetic. PKV allocates the per-layer past budget on a linear ramp from max=2​c−⌊c/20⌋\mathrm{max}=2c-\lfloor c/20\rfloor down by steps=⌊(max−min)/(L−1)⌋\mathrm{steps}=\lfloor(\mathrm{max}-\mathrm{min})/(L{-}1)\rfloor per layer, where c=B−wc=B-w and LL is the layer count. With Qwen’s L=28L{=}28 and B=64B{=}64 (c=56c{=}56) the floor lands on steps=4\mathrm{steps}{=}4, so the deepest layers keep only [14,10,6,2][14,10,6,2] past tokens—the last layer retains 22 tokens beside the 88-token window—whereas at B=32B{=}32 (steps=1\mathrm{steps}{=}1) the same layers keep [23,22,21,20][23,22,21,20]: the smaller budget leaves more cache in the deep layers, inverting the column. Qwen2.5-14B (L=48L{=}48) is the extreme case: at B=32B{=}32 the floor collapses to steps=0\mathrm{steps}{=}0, so the ramp degenerates and every layer keeps the flat max=47\mathrm{max}{=}47 past tokens—nearly twice the nominal budget—while at B=64B{=}64 (steps=2\mathrm{steps}{=}2) the deepest layer keeps only 1616. On L=32L{=}32 backbones the floor lands on steps=3\mathrm{steps}{=}3 at B=64B{=}64 (last layer 1717), so no inversion appears. Deferral is indifferent to this: SKV+Dge2+\textsc{Dge}_{2} is budget-invariant on Qwen (7B: 45.05/45.32/45.3245.05/45.32/45.32; 14B: 45.74/45.94/46.2745.74/45.94/46.27), so the artifact affects only the prefill-time schedule, not the timing result.

Per-dataset view of timing vs pseudo queries.

Figure 4(b) plots, per dataset at B=128B{=}128, SnapKV’s score against each method’s; points above y=xy{=}x beat SnapKV. Both timing methods (SKV++Dge2, SKV++Dge-W2) sit well above the diagonal and gain most on the hard, low-SnapKV summarization and code sets (clearing LAQ by +8.8+8.8 on GovReport), which they lift to FullKV level; Lookahead Q-Cache (m=16m{=}16, prefill-time) hugs the diagonal on exactly those sets, so its improvement is concentrated where SnapKV was already adequate.

Appendix M What the Diagnostics Ruled Out

Each alternative below was settled by the held-out probes of Appendix B in under a day of compute, before any LongBench run. We log them because the pattern is the point: every entry improves an in-window quantity and fails on held-out decode behavior—the same miscalibration §4 measures.

  • •

    Repeat-prefill selection. Re-forwarding the context to harvest “future-like” queries (the KVzip recipe, as a selection signal): −13%-13\% held-out coverage with mean run length 1.21.2—repetition queries attend to the locally-next token, shredding selection into singletons. Killed by the decode-replay coverage probe.

  • •

    Key-kernel mass-flow transport. Predicting where evicted attention mass re-flows from a key-similarity kernel (instead of the empirical co-attention TT of Appendix C): correlation with the true decode-time flow ≈0\approx 0. Killed by the offline transport-validation replay of Appendix C.

  • •

    Layer-only allocation. Re-allocating budget across layers without per-head granularity collapses the achievable held-out coverage gain from +8.0%+8.0\% (free per-head) to +2.7%+2.7\%: the variance that matters lives across heads, not layers. The free per-head variant is what Figure 2(a) plots on its allocate axis, under the family label cross-layer allocation: at its +8.0%+8.0\% coverage headroom a full sixteen-set run scores +0.60+0.60 LongBench over SnapKV, still under a point. Killed by the allocation headroom probe, which bounds the axis as a whole: on the same held-out split a better scoring signal is worth 4.44.4 points of βdec\beta_{\mathrm{dec}} against 0.70.7 for reallocating the per-head budget.

  • •

    Capped block waterfilling. Waterfilling the budget over fixed-size blocks with per-block caps: never separated from plain top-BB within noise at matched budgets, while adding a tunable. Dropped on the granularity ladder of Table 5.

  • •

    Per-token bias alone. The closed-form βi\beta_{i} of Appendix C without value absorption moves attention-output error by +1.5%+1.5\% at B=128B{=}128—the wrong way; re-weighting retained logits cannot restore mass whose value content is gone. Killed by the same offline replay that validates absorption (1111–14%14\%).
